utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Sir, do you hear me in your language? Now do you understand me while in the language you understand, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today, we continue to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Lattanzi being away due to her official duties. Sir, before you commence your evidence, I would like to let you know a couple of things. First thing is related to your protective measures. You will be testifying today with the benefit of the pseudonym and image and voice distortion. I was mistaken. You will have the image distortion only. Shall I show the witness the -- his image that will be broadcast outside? If the audio and video unit -- yes. This is how you will look outside. Do you understand that? And you will be referred to as your Witness number instead of your real name. Whenever we may discuss something that may reveal your identity, we will go into private session, which means what we discuss inside the courtroom will not be heard outside at all. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next, I must draw your attention to a certain rule, the rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in such circumstances, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled in such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will be pausing for interpretation and I kindly ask you to do the same.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up in e-court without being broadcast in public 1D09040?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kindly tell us, Witness, does this number tally with the name -- or, rather, is this your name?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the document under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I notice there's a mistake. It should be KW558.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will correct that and upload the correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we note that. You'll be called as KW558. Do you understand that? Yes, we will admit it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3762, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, have you testified in any other case and have you had an opportunity of reviewing your testimony in the course of the past days?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes. In 2004, in the month of January, it was the 23rd, the 24th of January, 2004, that I testified in the Blagojevic and Jokic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up in e-court 1D06910? And without it being publicly broadcast until we see if it's been redacted or not. Yes. It's a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the course of proofing with my Defence team, have you had an opportunity of reviewing the recording of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you come to the conclusion that what you stated at the time was properly recorded and was consistent with what you stated at the time?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: To the extent I was able to establish, it is consistent with my testimony at the time. And let me just note that I was a protected witness of the Prosecution at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today as had been put to you at the time in the courtroom, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: All the answers would essentially be the same as the ones from the previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the transcript into evidence pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although this first page is conducted in open session, I take it that part of this transcript contains private session testimony, therefore it should be put under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And we've also uploaded a public transcript which is 1D06955, so we would ask that they both be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering any associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are seven associated exhibits. We would ask that they also be added to our 65 ter list as we hadn't decided to use that testimony as the 92 ter material at the time we filed that exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Are there any objections, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both versions of the transcript will be admitted as well as the seven associated exhibits. Shall we assign the numbers in the order of the number of the 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 1D6910 will be D3763, under seal. 1D6955 will be Exhibit D3764. And the seven associated exhibits listed in the 92 ter notification will be assigned Exhibits D3765 through to Exhibit D3771 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the last item should be put under seal, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be placed under seal according to the comments in the notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I note there are two items, yes. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out the summary detailing the gist of the testimony of this witness in English. [In English] The Prosecution Witness KDZ065, whose evidence was admitted in this case in writing as Exhibit P336, claims that after his capture in Konjevic Polje on the morning of 13 of July 1995, the Witness KW558 took him to a nearby house where he was held prisoner. He also claims that Witness KW558 escorted him to an interrogatory -- interrogation by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. The summary of other witness's evidence is part of this witness's evidence, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Actually, I wrote this summary and these are the propositions that were put to the witness during his testimony in the Blagojevic case and then, as we indicate in the second paragraph of the summary, the witness refuted those. So this is, I think, a fair summary of what was -- what the transcript reveals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Costi, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Although this is not part of the evidence, I think it would be a good practice if the summary was the summary of the actual testimony of the witness rather than the case that was presented to the witness by the Prosecution or by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, can we not go directly to his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we could do that. If you would allow me, I could make a small summary of his evidence since we are going to have to depart from the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. President, Witness KW558 worked as a police officer and was present in Konjevic Polje on the morning of 13 July 1995. He has testified that he does not know the individual known as Prosecution Witness KDZ065 and that he did not transport him to a nearby house where that person claims to have been held prisoner. He also testified that he did not escort this witness to an interrogation by Bosnian Serb army officers in Konjevic Polje and did not hear of any or witness any beatings or execution of Bosnian Muslims during those events. He also testified that Nenad Deronjic was not working in Konjevic Polje on 13th of July, 1995, as far as he knows. And he never heard of any execution by the banks of the Jadar River. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. He also claims that KDZ065 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think the summary has been read out and that has been concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Excellency. So at that moment I do not have additional questions for Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may make one point, mention was made of me being there as a policeman. I wasn't there in the capacity of a policeman. I worked as a communications operator. I had never been a policeman, either before, during or after that period. I was a member of the MUP but, of course, there are other services that make up the MUP as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understood well -- shall I ask the Defence to clarify with the witness what he meant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency, but do we need private session for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been -- yes, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Your evidence has been admitted in writing, that is through your written transcript of testimony in the Blagojevic case, in lieu of your oral testimony, and now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: On 16 March 2001, you gave an interview to the Office of the Prosecutor, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Were they representatives of the Office of the Prosecutors or The Hague investigators on the 16th of March in Banja Luka? Well, I know that they were investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, yes. They were representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. And you told the truth during that interview, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sir, on 13 of July, you were in Konjevic Polje, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that you did not see any Muslim detainee with the exception of two, Hasan Salihovic, a former colleague of yours, and Resid Sinanovic. Right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes. His last name is not Selimovic, it's Salihovic. Hasan Salihovic, not Selimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: That's correct. My pronunciation might not have been accurate. Now, and you explain in your testimony that Mirko Peric from the Bratunac police and Dusko Neskovic from the Skelani police accompanied these two Muslim prisoners to the house where the communication room was. Right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you did recognise Hasan Salihovic as a former colleague of yours, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: No. Took them away. They brought them into the house where our command and communications centre were housed, and they brought the two men there. And we were there on the premises of the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: That must have been a translation issue because that's what I meant. They brought it to the house where you were. So and you showed some sympathy to Hasan because you said in your testimony you gave him food and cigarettes. Right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I gave them both to Hasan and to Sinanovic. Hasan was my colleague from pre-war period. We worked together at the police station in Zenica. He finished the secondary school of the interior with Nenad Deronjic. They were assigned to Gracac before Srebrenica, and then they came to Srebrenica to work there at the SJB for about a year and they worked there until the war broke out. Resid Sinanovic was brought by Mirko Peric before the war. He used to be a kind of manager at the SJB. I didn't know him, but Mirko Peric, having worked there, is the reason why they knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sure. And the -- so you showed some sympathy, you remember offering food and cigarettes to both of them, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Not only to Hasan. I offered this to Resid, cigarettes, coffee and whatever. Initially, I didn't recognise Hasan because I used to see him in uniform. Now he was wearing an old suit, civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you had a conversation with Hasan and then you told him to relax because he was quite agitated. This is what you said in your testimony, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: It was not properly translated. He was not agitated. He was terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you tried to help him to relax. In fact, in your testimony you said, and I quote your testimony in what you said to Hasan, you said: Please relax, just that we were sitting together in 1992, together when we were having coffee together in the police station, when we were colleagues, right? This is --

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I literally said: Hasko, feel as if what the two of us used to do before the war, at the police station. We are having coffee together, don't be afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: If I may add, because before the war, communications centre was part of the Srebrenica CJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, in during this conversation you also asked Hasan why he surrendered, and Hasan told you that he couldn't bear anymore the situation because his son, brothers and father had been killed?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: No. That's -- well, the essence of our conversation was I asked him: Hasko, didn't you go to Tuzla before the war, because I remained working in Srebrenica up until the 17th of April, 1992, and then at one point, I'm talking about this specific period, I think he had a wife and two children and he drove them to Gradacac because that's where his wife came from. I think that he also wanted to take his parents as well and I thought that he had gone there. And then all of a sudden, when he appeared in 1995, I was surprised to see him. May I? He told me that he had managed to take his wife and children to Gradacac, that he went back to drive his parents away, but since there were roadblocks, he couldn't make it and they remained in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you didn't ask him why he surrendered at that point? I understand that part of the conversation --

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: No, no, no. I asked him because I was convinced, I thought -- and I was surprised to see him there. I was convinced that he had left in 1992 together with his parents. In 1992, Srebrenica was an empty town in the month of April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We've already mentioned Mirko Peric of the Bratunac police. Now, as you may know, Mirko Peric provided a statement to the Karadzic Defence and he also gave an interview to the Bosnian Serb MUP in 2003, and in both testimony he said that in the room, when he brought Resid Sinanovic, he saw some other Muslims. Or to use the words, the language that he used in the interview: "I saw some other people detained there." So even one of your colleagues recalls that in the house where you were, the communication room, there were other detainees. So I'm asking it again, do you recall other Muslim detainees being held there together with Resid and Hasan?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I don't remember that at all, no, I don't remember. I only know about those two, that they were offered food, that we were sitting and talking, that he was describing the situation in Srebrenica and so on. He told us that one kilo of salt was about 100 German marks, the price of the coffee, that the living conditions were awful. As for any others, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me move on, then. Let me show you two documents, two regular combat reports of the 5th Engineering Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 03840, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, the one you will see appearing on your screen is a combat report on 12th of July of the 5th Engineering Battalion. And if we go on the first page of both English and B/C/S, and we look at number 2, letter F, it says: "The MUP police company carries out tasks upon order of his command, deploying patrols and setting up ambushes in the area of Konjevic Polje." So the MUP police task was to setting ambushes and capturing Muslim in the area of Konjevic Polje, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So this document is inaccurate and wrong as well?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: No. Our specific tasks, and before the 6th Company, other companies, police companies, used to go to Konjevic Polje. We were deployed there on the 4th of July. That's what the order said. Before us, the 5th Company had been there, since March.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 12th of July now --

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: If I may tell you this, and then I will tell you about this as well. Until March 1995, the army was holding and securing the area. In March, the public security centre of Zvornik took over and various companies, the 1st, the 2nd, the 4th, the 5th were deployed. Before us there was the 5th Company and then finally the 6th Company was deployed there. The tasks of the police at the time were purely to secure the check-point in Konjevic Polje at the intersection that was held by the SJB in order to control the smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Shall we talk about the 12th now --

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: And it all lasted until the problems around Srebrenica arose, so these were purely civilian tasks and let me add this --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you -- sorry. I have limited time so I really ask you to focus on my questions. We are looking at a document of the 12th of July, it's talking about the MUP task in the area of Konjevic Polje, and I'm asking you whether it is accurate or not that MUP police carried out tasks including ambushing the Muslim in the area of Konjevic Polje. The answer is simple, "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: The 6th Company, no. The 6th Company took care purely of civilian affairs and was providing support to the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And what about the other companies --

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: -- officers at the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Were there other MUP company engaged in these activities?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Up until the 12th, no, there were no such things. But as for later, I don't know who was deployed where because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: On the 12th, there was no MUP company engaged in this activity? This document is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I'm talking about my company, the 6th Company. As for the others, no, I'm only talking about the 6th Company that had 22 members.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, can I ask this document to be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6432, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Can we clarify whether this is a document that originated from the army or from the police? This 5th Engineers Battalion, was it part of the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm asking the Prosecutor to kindly clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Costi --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: It is from the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- yes, clarified it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have now P00247, please. This is another document from the same 5th Engineering Battalion, another combat report, this time on the 14 of July, so two days later. And at point 1, first page of both English and B/C/S, it says: "A large enemy group was infiltrated in the region of Budo Brado [phoen] and the region of Konjevic Polje. Units of the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP successfully resisted the enemy. About a thousand to 1,500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So in light of these two documents, the first one which you don't know whether it was going on, what was going on with other MUP police company, one indicated it was setting up ambushes, the other indicates that 1.000, 1.500 civilians were arrested, and soldiers, and killed. You were saying that when you were in Konjevic Polje, you saw two Muslims, no one else? 1.000, 1.500 in this area, and you saw two Muslims surrendering and being arrested in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Konjevic Polje is a broad notion. It encompasses a large area. My location and where my command was -- location was a small house with two storeys. This is where the communication centre was. What was happening further afield, especially towards Pobudje and other places, I had no knowledge of that because I had no possibility of knowing. After the 13th and the 14th, probably police units remained there who were connected with the army, but I cannot talk about that because I wasn't there and I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So let's talk about these two Muslims you had contacts with, Hasan Salihovic and Resid Sinanovic. Now, both in your testimony in Blagojevic and in your interview with the OTP, you said that they were brought there to be protected. And in particular in your interview with the OTP on 16 March 2001, at page 18 and 19, you said this: "Now, reportedly these two, Sinanovic Resid and Salihovic Hasan, were brought there with intention to be saved, as far as I know, because Salihovic Hasan was also a colleague of Dusko and he used to work with him together, and Sinanovic Resid used to be the chief of Peric Mirko in Bratunac. "Q. Explain what do you mean by 'they were brought there to be saved'? "A. They were brought there -- they brought them there with that purpose. "Q. Save them from who? "A. Probably from these who went there to -- um, what do I know, to ..." So I'd like to clarify this point and let me ask you a series of question. First of all, you didn't want them to be killed, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you believed or those who brought it to you believed that it wasn't safe to leave them outside in the hands of the police or the military who captured them, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: For them not to be maltreated, in that respect. In order to save them from being maltreated they were put away and they were brought to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you wanted to protect them from other police or military that might have maltreated them, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who could have maltreated them. It could have been anyone, a soldier, a policeman, a civilian. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, they are in the hands of the military when they were captured or other police. And there are no paramilitaries in the area, right? There is no paramilitaries in 1995 July in this area?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I don't know to whom they were handed over because I wasn't there --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: That's why you said --

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: -- these two know who they handed them over to.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not overlap, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So either MUP or police -- or, sorry, either MUP or military, these were the two forces acting in that point in that area, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Most probably that's right. There were both the army and the police there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you want --

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: But I don't know all of them who were there, with the exception of members of my unit, and certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you know them or not. I'm just -- you agreed that there was either the police or the military that were there. So you wanted to protect them from them because you knew they might have been mistreated or killed, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Not me, because I myself wasn't there. There was the two of those men who recognised them, and between our command and the intersection from which they were brought, the distance is about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me ask it again. You said that you wanted to protect them, so you wanted -- you believed yourself that there was a risk. You just said it, they might have been mistreated by either the military or the police?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: When they brought them to the command where we were, Dusko and Mirko, they literally said in order to avoid them being maltreated, let them be there because they were colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you are also aware that they might have been killed, right? You also wanted to avoid that someone who wanted to kill them among the police and the military could actually kill them?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: At the time, I did not even dream that something like that could happen, things that happened later on, especially the things mentioned at the trial of Milosevic. But at that particular time, we were 1.000 per cent sure that those men would be exchanged, that everything would be carried out according to a normal procedure, and that they wouldn't be harmed in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, the remains of both Hasan Salihovic and Resid Sinanovic were then found in mass graves. You know that, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Well, I did hear of it. I don't know the precise circumstances. I did hear that their mortal remains were recovered. But that was after a long, long time. I didn't know what became of them for a very long time. They spent an hour perhaps there with us, an hour and a half at the most. Momir Nikolic arrived then. He was a security officer in the Bratunac Brigade, along with another officer, a policeman I didn't know. They came in and asked where the two were. The door was opened to the corridor. There was a bed there. Hasan was seated on the other end where there was a bench and I was seated in front. The communication between Resid and Momir was such that revealed to me that they knew each other well from before. He didn't know Hasan, though. The communication had to do with the situation up in the woods, the head count.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So let me move to another topic now. In your statement you said that Nenad Deronjic was occasionally in Konjevic Polje, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Nenad Deronjic was working for the Bratunac public security station from the beginning of the war and Bratunac held the check-point at Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your extended testimony has been admitted in written form so I would kindly ask you to, as far as you can, to stick with short answer to my questions. So the question was whether he was occasionally in Konjevic Polje and you said yes. Right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes. He manned the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you also said in your testimony at page 38 that it is possible that Nenad Deronjic was there on the 10th and 11th of July, right? Please --

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: It was so long ago so it's difficult for me to say, but there were shifts that he worked in, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. and then from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. Now, was it the 10th or the 11th, I don't know. He worked in shifts so he would have days off. Now, on that day --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Then you say there was an order for the Zvornik centre, security centre, an order according to which policemen who worked in Srebrenica before the war should report to the Srebrenica SJB, right? And you said that Nenad Deronjic was one of them, former police from Srebrenica who was ordered by the Zvornik security centre to go back to Srebrenica, right? Yes or no? Yes?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you also explained that this order is the reason why you supposed he went to Srebrenica, and at page 38, let me read what you said: "And Deronjic was one of the current employees of the Srebrenica police station so I suppose he went back too. I don't remember seeing him around at the time that this event involving Sinanovic and Salihovic -- of the event involving Sinanovic and Salihovic."

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And Salihovic. So you assumed that he went to Srebrenica because -- you suppose he went back too because there was this order for him to go, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you also said that you don't know when he actually reported to Srebrenica, and I read what you said at page 23: "But I don't know when exactly he went there."

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I have -- sorry, P06429, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, the one you will see appearing on the screen is the order you are referring to. And it's an order --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I don't see the English but -- it's -- thank you. It's an order from the Zvornik CJB to the Bratunac SJB, order by Vasic, and it said: "Due to the need for the establishment of police station in Srebrenica, upon its liberation, and pursuant to the approval of the Deputy Minister of Interior, I hereby issue the following order. The below listed policemen who had previously worked at the Srebrenica SJB are to be sent immediately, by 21st July 1995 at the latest, to the Srebrenica SJB where the station chief in coordination with the officer in charge from the Zvornik CJB shall assign them to their duties and tasks." And then number 3, you can see Nenad Deronjic. So as you said, Nenad Deronjic was deployed to the Srebrenica SJB. As you said, he was selected because he was a former policeman from Srebrenica. However, the order was issued on 18 July and he was requested to report by the 21st of July. So you testified that you were not sure when he exactly went to Srebrenica. This document answered your question. He went to Srebrenica by the end of July, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I don't know when he left. I can't make any assertions about that, was it on the 12th or any other day. The only thing I know is that, number 1, on the 13th of July, an order arrived that all the employees who used to work in the Srebrenica public security station should head to Srebrenica so that a police station may be set up in order to protect the essential institutions and in view of the prevailing chaos in Srebrenica at the time. Now, I'm not clear on what this is on this date. All the police employees from Skelani went over there, and Zdravko, my colleague, was an encryption operator, so that at the time only one policeman stayed back in Skelani, and that was too few and we couldn't cover all the police duties. So I'm not familiar with this particular situation. I'm telling you this on the basis of what the commander told us earlier and I'm talking about the company commander. He was the commander of the Skelani police station.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you're saying that on 13 of July there was another order for former Srebrenica police to go to Srebrenica? Although not even Nenad Deronjic testified about that. He testified that he ended his shift and he went to Bratunac and he was told only in the afternoon that he had to report to Srebrenica and not to the police station but as PJP. So you're saying now that there is another order that we are not aware of and not even Nenad Deronjic is aware of?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I don't know if it was there or not. I'm telling you what the company commander told us, that a police station should be set up in Srebrenica and that all those who before the war used to work in the police station in Srebrenica had to head to Srebrenica. So I can't claim whether Nenad was in Srebrenica or in Bratunac on that critical date. He was supposed to be in Srebrenica, as were other members of the pre-war Srebrenica police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Isn't it true, though, that the only order we see is requiring Nenad Deronjic to be in Srebrenica on the 21st of July and it was issued on the 18 of July and you have it in front of you? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I have an objection here. This should probably be stated outside the presence of the witness, but this examination I think is very misleading for a reason that if I were to reveal it, it could potentially impact on the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has a question for you, Mr. Robinson -- no. I'll ask Mr. Costi first. Do you need that question? Only order to confirm with the witness? If you are maintaining your position, we will excuse the witness and hear the objection from Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I would say that it is a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. So we need to go into private session and then we need to draw the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have to go into private session but we have to install the blinds -- draw the blinds. I will explain to -- just a second. Sir, we have something to discuss with the parties in your absence. So if you could excuse yourself for some moments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I believe that there is an order issued by Dragomir Vasic on the 12th of July, 1995, in which he orders that the police are to be assembled in Bratunac and taken to the Srebrenica -- to open a police station. And so I think the Prosecution is well aware of that order. I don't -- I've been looking for it in e-court in the few minutes that I've had and I haven't been able to find the number, but I think Mr. Nicholls certainly knows that. And anyway, so to put a question to the witness that the only document requiring Nenad Deronjic to be in Srebrenica was issued on 18 July is really misleading when there is an order to staff the Srebrenica police station as of the afternoon of the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe Mr. Robinson refers to P04935, and that this point 5 reads: "Acting upon the President Karadzic's order which was conveyed to us today over the phone, the 2nd Company of the Zvornik PJP shall be dispatched to Srebrenica with the task of securing facilities important for the town." And we dealt with it yesterday with Mr. Deronjic. The reason why I think my line of questioning is fair is because the first time an order for the former police coming from Srebrenica to go to Srebrenica to the SJB came only on the 18 of July. On the basis of the series of documents we saw yesterday, the Zvornik CJB asked the Srebrenica SJB which were the former employees, the Srebrenica SJB answered, and then the Zvornik CJB issued an order. Now, the witness recalls that Nenad Deronjic had to leave because he was a former police from Srebrenica. So the basis of his recollection is that, like him, he's a former police from Srebrenica. Now, the decision of sending former policemen from Srebrenica to Srebrenica and the order came only on the 18th. Now, on the 12th, the 2nd PJP which might have included Nenad Deronjic as we discussed yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this witness's evidence was, whether he saw this decision or not, he heard from his company commander irrespective of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: But my point was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So he -- was he in the position to tell you definitely whether this is the only order he received or not. So that's the point of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, I was responding to Mr. Robinson's objections. But to answer your question, Your Honour, he might not be in a position to definitely answer, I agree, but I think it was fair to confront him with the fact that the selection of former policemen from Srebrenica came up later, so his recollection that happened on the 12th is wrong. I didn't mean to have from this witness the ultimate answer as whether this issue was discussed before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson, do you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the proposition that the Prosecution is putting to the witness is a false one so this -- they have evidence that on the 12th, the Srebrenica police station was staffed by the MUP and a number of police officers went there. We can dispute whether or not Nenad Deronjic was one of them or not, but then to say that the only order that was issued to send policemen to Srebrenica was on the 18th is misleading. That order may very well have been for the formal staffing of the police that was to take place on a permanent basis, but the reality is that on the 12th, that police station was staffed with people. So I believe that the Prosecution's question is putting a premise to the witness which could mislead him and which is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you agree that the document you referred to is Exhibit P4935?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, it may be P2995. My document dated the 12th of July. P2995. I do believe that under that same number, we have a supplement by Deputy Kovac which clearly says as of 12 July, the station is to be set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The document you referred to is a document from the MUP, and the one referred to by Mr. Robinson was from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just ask one -- add one comment. I was going back to my question and there is no dispute that there was an order on the 12th to establish the Srebrenica SJB but that wasn't my question, nor I suggest that it was established later. My question was: Isn't it true, though, that the only order we see is require -- that requiring Nenad Deronjic to be in Srebrenica is requiring Nenad Deronjic to be in Srebrenica on the 21st and it was issued on the 18 of July. That was my question and this I don't believe is misleading at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, as far as you concentrate on the issue of selection of former policemen from Srebrenica, the Chamber sees no difficulty with it. Shall we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for the witness, Your Excellencies, may I draw your attention to P2994, my order dated the 11th of July. P2995 is a document where the MUP is conveying the order on the 12th of July. So the sequence of events is as follows: I issued an order on the 11th, and the MUP passed it over to its entire area within its jurisdiction on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is aware of those sequence of orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we lift the blinds first? Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Yes, Mr. Costi, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So I will repeat my question to you. Isn't it true that the first order to Nenad Deronjic to be deployed to the Srebrenica SJB as one of the former police officers of the Srebrenica SJB before the war was issued on the 18th of July and required him to report to Srebrenica on 21st of July?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: At the time I was in Konjevic Polje, and it may have been the 13th or the 14th because I left either on the 14th or the 15th, this paper was not available to me to read it, nor was it the case later when I went towards Skelani. Nenad Deronjic, apart from being a member of the Srebrenica police station before the war, he was also a member of the Special Police Unit – was it the Second, the Third Company? He was a younger person. I only know that they were supposed to go up there. Was he there in the capacity of a member of the Special Police Unit? Was it in that capacity that he left? I don't know. I don't know the date itself or time. I only know that I didn't see him with my own eyes on the 13th at Konjevic Polje. Previously, before problems emerged around Srebrenica, I know that he was manning the check-point over there on regular police duty, and also in Bratunac. So I can’t claim that he was in Srebrenica. I can only tell you that I didn't see him, I personally, on the 13th in Konjevic Polje, where I was. I do know about this. I know that they were supposed to be up there. Now, was it in this capacity or in his capacity as a member of a company within the Special Police Unit, I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm just wondering if there is a translation error and maybe it can be clarified. On line 25, on page 34, that is completely opposite of what he's been saying before. I seem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sir, did you see Nenad Deronjic on the 13th at Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I state upon full responsibility I did not, not where I was, in the HQ of the 6th Police Company. 90 per cent of my time on that day I did spend on the premises of that HQ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where did you see him at all in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the 13th, he worked at the check-point operated by the Bratunac public security station at the intersection in Konjevic Polje. He worked there with other policemen. There were two or three of them normally, and they would be checking for illegal smuggling of goods but I'm telling you that this happened before the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will ask the CLSS to hear that audio recording but I will ask you again whether this is correct transcription of what you said. Our transcript says like this, I quote: It's about Nenad Deronjic. "Was he there in the capacity of a member of the Special Police Company? Was it in that capacity that he left? I don't know. I don't know the date itself. Was it the 13th or the 14th? I only know that I didn't see him in Skelani at all, whereas, as for the check-point at Konjevic Polje" -- could you hear it out and then tell us what you really said? Please hear it out with care. "Was it the 13th or the 14th? I only know that I didn't see him in Skelani at all, whereas, as for the check-point at Konjevic Polje, I know that he was manning the check-point over there, and he was in Bratunac. So I can't claim that he was in Srebrenica. I can only tell you that I didn't see him. I only saw him on the 13th at Konjevic Polje. I do know about this. I know that he was supposed to be up there. Now, was it in this capacity or the capacity of his membership in the Special Police Company, I don't know. I wasn't there."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is quite a few mistakes there. Mention is made of, in that quotation, Skelani, in interpretation. I didn't mention Skelani. I was talking about Konjevic Polje. And then at one point it said that I saw him on the 13th, which I didn't say. That was misinterpreted. I was able to see him only before the 13th, the 10th or the 11th, before all these events. I can't recall. It was a long time ago, and I could have seen him as a person manning the check-point. As for the 13th and the subsequent days, I don't know where he was. I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wonder whether this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer would you need, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I would say about 20, 30 minutes. I'm not sure how much time left I have, to be honest. I think I have 20 minutes and I will do it in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00 -- yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I don't want to delay the break. I just have to say that was, in my view, a completely inappropriate intervention by Mr. Robinson. It's one thing for Mr. Karadzic, who speaks both languages, to suggest a translation error, but for Mr. Robinson to say, "I think there may have been a translation error because now the witness is saying something different than he said before" is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I completely disagree. The witness showed that there was a translation error. What would be inappropriate is for the Prosecution to have taken advantage of an error like that and have the Chamber be relying on misinformation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Besides, I did try to intervene but I wasn't given an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, because I noted it, I asked Mr. Robinson to offer his view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But the Prosecution's point is not without merit, and we would know why if we translated it into our own jurisdictions. This isn't a jury trial so it's not the same thing but it would be better for the avoidance of doubt if these interpretation issues came solely from Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, let's change topic. In your interview that you gave to the Prosecution in 2001, you said that your position as a communication person was to stay inside the house in the communication room where the communication equipment was. And you said that you rarely left the house and you would occasionally go to the check-point to get some water. Right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: In your Blagojevic --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: In your Blagojevic testimony you also described and said that the window that was in the room wouldn't allow you to see what was happening in the street. Right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: The vision was restricted because the house faced the road, which led from the crossroads from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. On the right-hand side, there was a larger building which had been partly destroyed and from there or around -- rather, because of that you couldn't see the check-point and what was happening there. And from the command to the check-point, the distance was about 200 metres, but I'm not really sure. You had to go to the main road and then you had to turn right to reach the check-point at the crossroads of the roads leading from Zvornik to Milici and the other leading from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And in fact, in your testimony -- or, rather, in your interview with the OTP, there are a series of things that you said you couldn't see. You were asked whether you noticed a concentration of policemen and troops at Konjevic Polje who arrived with buses and trucks, and you answer: "I don't know that, they could have been but I didn't see that." And later on, you were asked that other witness have told us that there was a lot of prisoner waiting for transportation, being guarded by soldier in the field here around Konjevic Polje, and you answered: "No, I don't know anything about that. Maybe they were there but I didn't go to that part. I didn't see them. Maybe they were there. Maybe they surrendered but I didn't see them." And finally, your testimony in the Blagojevic case, at page 23, you were asked the following: "Now, as we understand it, at some point on the 13th, General Mladic came by the area. Do you recall seeing General Mladic and his entourage? "A. I didn't see him. Maybe the men who were at the check-point or around the check-point at that time could have seen him, but not me. I spent most of the time on the premises in the house I described and I did not see him. He might have passed through but I did not see him." So my question for you is: On the morning of the 13th, there was nothing different. Did you walk around or you stayed most of the time inside the house?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I spent most of the time in the house and around the house, but mostly in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So from where you were then in the house, you could not see what was happening in the warehouse at the crossroad, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: As you said, it was about 200 metres. And from where you were, I take it, you could not see what was happening on the bank of the Jadar River either. Right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: No. I couldn't see because the Jadar River is far from us and there is no chance that I could have seen things going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber heard testimony and took notice of adjudicated facts that 16 Bosnian Muslim men including one boy had been captured from the column and transferred by bus from Konjevic Polje, from the warehouse, to the Jadar River bank, and there the men got off the bus, they were lined up and executed, and only one survived. Now, do you know is it true, isn't it, that that morning men were shot in a mass execution at the Jadar River?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were member of the Skelani SJB or, let's say, attached to the Skelani SJB, right?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I was a member of the Skelani SJB. I was involved in communications and cryptic protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, in your interview in 2001 at page 36, you said that you heard later from the media that Muslims had been executed in Kravica. You said: "I don't know, as far as myself personally, I haven't seen anything as for that, but as far as for rumours, some things were mentioned, whether with Kravica or Luka, there was many of these people were executed there. But who executed them, on what date, what time, I don't know that. I don't know. I haven't seen that personally." "Q. Who told you about this? "A. Lately, it was mentioned, even in the public. It was broadcast publicly in the media. And also when Alija Izetbegovic came to Srebrenica, to the car battery's factory, I think it was on that news." And a few lines below: "But I wasn't there, really, I don't know that. I wasn't there and I don't know." So my first question is, when did you first hear of what happened, of the executions at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: When the cornerstone of the memorial centre in Potocari was supposed to be laid out by Alija Izetbegovic, I don't know when that was exactly. At first in Srebrenica, there was only the OBN television. And when that gathering took place in Potocari, at the place of the current memorial centre, Alija Izetbegovic held a speech, then there was a reference to Kravica and it was only then that things started being mentioned about Kravica, about people having been killed there. I don't know when that was, in 2000-something. So when that cornerstone was first laid in Potocari for the memorial centre and when he arrived, I heard that on television, on the OBN channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you heard of Kravica for the first time in 2000-something. You know that a policeman from Skelani on the 13 of July, Krsto Dragicevic, was killed in Kravica, in the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I learned that subsequently, when he had been killed. At the time when that was happening, I didn't know. He was a member of the company of the police of the Special Police from Sekovici. Their platoon was up there in Skelani. And as to what happened, where he was killed, how he was killed, I didn't know that in -- at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 6, the witness said: "Later on, I learned where he had been killed," not "when he had been killed." So it should be "where" instead of "when."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you said "later on." You mean around 2000, when you also heard of the execution, or later on, meaning days later, month later, later on, later what?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: A few days later, I heard from people in Konjevic Polje. I was the first to leave my company on the 14th, the 15th or the 16th. I'm -- I don't know when exactly. You will probably find it in the record. The chief of the communications centre of the public security centre in Zvornik came. We were in that command. And he told me, and I don't want to mention my name, he told me, You have to go to Skelani. Why? Because there was nobody in the communication centre in Skelani in the police station, there is just one policeman. I don't know whether that was on the 14th, the 15th or the 16th of July. I don't know. When I arrived in Skelani, I learned that Krsto had been killed. I also learned that he had been buried in Skelani. He hailed from somewhere around Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So your testimony is that from the 15, 16 July 1995, until the 2000, you did not get any information, more precise, about what happened to your colleague and to the Muslims at the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: On the 14th, the 15th or the 16th of July 1995, that's when I arrived in Skelani from Konjevic Polje, whereas my other colleagues remained there for a while. So I don't know what had happened in Kravica. I didn't know that. And the distance between Kravica and Konjevic Polje is over 30 kilometres. I don't know exactly how far it is, how far the two are from each other. Kravica is approximately halfway between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: We know Kravica and Konjevic Polje -- and Skelani are quite far from each other, and one witness who testified here, Dane Katanic, you probably know him, he testified that he learned right on the 13th that -- he heard of the killings at the Kravica warehouse, and he learned that -- not just that Krsto was killed but the Muslims were killed because one policeman of their town was killed. So you're saying you haven't heard about it for three days and then you learned the Muslims were killed only five years later? Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know that, if that had indeed happened, and I didn't know because if people had done that, why do you think that somebody would be talking about how they did it and what had happened? So I didn't know. And if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me just ask you the question. And when you learned that Krsto was killed, what were you told? In which circumstances was he killed?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I don't know, after such a long time. I don't know how I learned, who told me. After such a long time I can't remember. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm not sure about you -- I don't care about who told you but what were you told?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: How shall I put it? He was not our colleague. He was a colleague but not from our police station. He was a special. They were on the other side of Skelani. They were totally separated from us. We did not have any tasks in common. Our policemen in Skelani were engaged in civilian policing and they were specials. They were a platoon of the Special Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you were told Krsto has been killed and then no information about execution or killing of the Muslims, and then five years later, when you saw Izetbegovic in Potocari for the memorial, in [indiscernible] of memorial, you finally realised that a thousand Muslims were killed that day, a few kilometres from Konjevic Polje in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I stand by the statement that I gave at the time. At that time, I didn't know what had happened in Kravica, if anything had happened at all and how things had transpired. Moreover, at the time of the Milosevic trial, I was watching television and I heard of some things for the first time after such a long time. I didn't have a clue what had been going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I have two minutes left and I have just one last question. Now, today you seems to doubt about the date when you drove back from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. In the interview you gave to the Prosecution, you said: "On the 14th, it was -- I think it was on the 14th, in the morning hours, perhaps around 9.00, I went to Bratunac." So you did drive on the 14th back to Bratunac? Do you stand by what you said to the Prosecution in 2001?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: After such a long time, I can't tell you whether it was on the 14th, the 15th or the 16th. I don't know the exact date. However, I know that I left before noon, upon the orders of the chief of the communications centre from the public communications centre in Zvornik. He told me that I had to go to Skelani, he drove me to the bridge in Bratunac, and from there, I proceeded towards Skelani because allegedly there was just one policeman there and there was nobody in the communications centre. All the other policemen had gone to Srebrenica, to set up a police station in Srebrenica. That was the reason why they had all gone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So I take it from the way -- on the way back to Bratunac you haven't seen what other witnesses, Defence witnesses, testified about in this case, pile of bodies in front of the Kravica warehouse, traffic jam of buses with soldiers in front of the Kravica warehouse, and later on, trucks removing bodies and bringing them to Glogova, which is also on your way to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: At that time, as I was passing through, I did not notice anybody. And we just discussed the reasons for which I had to go to Skelani. I had not seen my family for a number of days, so I was reluctant to go there. That's what we were talking about on the way to Bratunac. I had not seen my family and my children for some 10 to 15 days. They were in exile in Ljubovija. He told me, You have to go, there's nobody else. That's what we were talking about. A long story short, I had to go there because after my field mission I was supposed to be given a few days off to spend with my family, three or four days, so I did not pay attention to what was going on around me so that's what we mostly talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I think my time is up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please tell us how frequent were burials on the Serbian side at that time? How frequently killings happened?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: Where do you mean, in Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the entire area of Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: There were a lot of burials at that time in that area, and one of those burials took place on the 21st, the 22nd or the 23rd of June at Kragivoda. An ambush was set up for the members of our police station, two of our -- two of the army members Ostoja Bozic and Dragisa Pavlovic were on the way back in a van. There was an ambush, they were killed and massacred. That's when that burial took place. Perhaps on the 23rd, 24th or 25th of July. I believe it was on the 23rd of June was when that ambush happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And between the 23rd of June and the 13th of July, were there any casualties on the Serbian side at the hands of the locals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know where this line of questioning is going, but as it stands now, it's not an issue that was arisen -- rise during the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I just wanted to see whether it was the wonder of all wonders that Krsto was killed. Was that a striking event or whether that was an everyday occurrence. I have to leave this topic now that -- after I've been asked to provide an explanation myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please move on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever guard prisoners as a guard? Did you ever do that and when?

utterances.speaker: KW558
utterances.text: I was never a guard. And I guarantee that. I was not a policeman, although that is also mentioned at places. From the 1st of January, 1989, I was involved in communications and encryption. I was never a guard. I was never a policeman. When I served in the JNA I was also a communications man, when I served in the army in 1978 and 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Witness, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. But we'll have a short break to change the setting. I think five minutes would do. We'll have a break for five minutes, and resume at 20 to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peric. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Peric, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled in such circumstances, would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please take care to make pauses between questions and answers and to speak as slowly as possible so that everything can be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, could you come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters could hear you well? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was quite fast. Please pause a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 1D9070 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, can you see that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the last page so that he can identify his signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement accurately and faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today, live, would your answers basically be the same as the ones contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be completely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3772, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going now to read a summary of Mr. Mirko Peric's statement in English. [In English] Mirko Peric refutes the testimony of Prosecution Witness KDZ065 in several respects. He states that he was a police officer working at a check-point in Konjevic Polje on 13th of July, 1995, but never escorted any prisoner to a warehouse, never observed prisoners being beaten, never heard of any prisoners being transported by a woman bus driver to the bank of the Jadar River, and never heard of any prisoners being executed in the area. Mirko Peric states that he did not see Nenad Deronjic in Konjevic Polje on 13th of July, 1995, as claimed by the Prosecution Witness KDZ065. Mirko Peric states that while working at the check-point at Konjevic Polje, he was looking at all the drivers of the buses as they were passing by. He never saw or heard of any woman bus driver working at that time as claimed by Prosecution Witness KDZ065. That would have been very unusual and he would have noticed it if it were true. Thank you. At this point, I have no questions for Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Peric, as you have noted, your evidence-in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written witness statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Costi?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: In your statement, at paragraph 13, you said that you were sent to Konjevic Polje on the 10th or the 11th of July, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you said that you remained there for three days, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you went back to Bratunac on the 13th or the 14th, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: I am not 100 per cent sure about the date. I spent there three or four days in that period, so let's say between the 9th and then 10th, 11th or 12th, but I cannot give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, did you go to the warehouse and intersection of the roads on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: You also said that you left to attend the funeral of your mother-in-law, if I'm not mistaken. Do you recall which day was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: I believe it was the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So your statement is inaccurate when you said that you went to Konjevic Polje either the 10th or the 11th, as you said now, so you were in Konjevic Polje before, 9, 10, 11, one of these days?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO PERIC
utterances.text: I told you I cannot give you the exact dates. Anyway, I was in Konjevic Polje in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you said that in those days, you did not see Nenad Deronjic, and I read you paragraph 20 of your statement: "During my stay in Konjevic Polje, I did not see Dragisa Zekic outside the house where our communications were. As far as I know, he was not allowed to leave the house. And during that time I also did not see Nenad Deronjic in Konjevic Polje." So you haven't seen Nenad Deronjic in those days, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think so. We can --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary because that discussion was in private session, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, Nenad Deronjic testified that he was in Konjevic Polje in fact on the 10th, 11th -- I'm sorry? I'm sorry, I think the answer to my prior question did not go into the record. I asked whether he confirmed his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, correct, because of Mr. Karadzic's intervention. You didn't see Nenad Deronjic in those days? What was your answer, Mr. Peric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certain that in those days I did not see Nenad Deronjic in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, we will redact your intervention, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So my next point was that Nenad Deronjic testified here that he was indeed in Konjevic Polje on the 10th, on the 11th, and then he left on the morning on the 12th.
